slides.title: A Christmas project named after a comedy troupe

items.cap: Guido van Rossum - photo: Daniel Stroud, CC BY-SA 4.0

items: December 1989: a hobby interpreter for a closed office
Named for Monty Python's Flying Circus - not the snake
February 1991: version 0.9.0 posted to alt.sources
Three decades of 'Benevolent Dictator For Life' followed

items.who: Guido van Rossum, at CWI in Amsterdam
items.where: released to the alt.sources newsgroup as version 0.9.0

slides.notes:
STORY (1989-12 to 1991-02): Over the 1989 Christmas break, a researcher at the Dutch CWI institute started a hobby interpreter to keep himself busy while the office was closed. He named it after Monty Python's Flying Circus, not the snake. In February 1991 he posted version 0.9.0 to the alt.sources newsgroup, and for the next three decades served as the language's 'Benevolent Dictator For Life'. Every prompt on these slides is that hobby project, grown up.
SOURCE: Python's documented history: project begun December 1989 at CWI; 0.9.0 posted to alt.sources in February 1991; summarized with references at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_van_Rossum. Photo: Daniel Stroud, CC BY-SA 4.0.

slides.title: The interpreter sheds its oldest lock
slides.sub: accepted 2023-07; optional builds since Python 3.13

items: For decades one lock let a single thread run Python at a time
July 2023: the Steering Council accepts PEP 703 - the lock becomes optional
Since Python 3.13, free-threaded builds ship beside the standard ones

items.label: not trivia - THIS interpreter answers about its own lock

items.who: Sam Gross's design, accepted by the Python Steering Council as PEP 703
items.where: peps.python.org - and the interpreter running these slides

slides.notes:
STORY (accepted 2023-07; optional builds since Python 3.13): For most of Python's life a Global Interpreter Lock let only one thread run Python code at a time. In July 2023 the Steering Council accepted PEP 703, built on Sam Gross's work, making the lock optional; free-threaded builds have shipped beside the standard ones since Python 3.13. This is not trivia from a changelog: the gil console on these slides asks the interpreter in front of you whether its lock is on, and prints what it answers.
SOURCE: PEP 703 'Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython', author Sam Gross, accepted by the Steering Council in July 2023 (peps.python.org/pep-0703); the deck's gil console reads sys._is_gil_enabled() from the build interpreter.
NOTE: the build interpreter answered _is_gil_enabled() = True.
slides.take: Modern practice is checkable - ask your own interpreter
